en: The Mausala Parva (The Book of the Staff)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jayamudīrayet).
While the illustrious Dharmarāja, the foremost among kings, was ruling the earth,
the highly fortunate sages went to Dvārakā in his twenty-sixth year.
Seeing those led by Kauśika, the bulls among the Vṛṣṇis— overflowing with the intoxication of great joy— dressed Sāmba in the attire of a bride and questioned him.
"O lords of sages, will she have a son or a daughter?
Having heard that, they said: "She will be the death of her family."
Having said, "The mace is called the Brahma-staff," they vanished from sight;
thereafter, Sāmba brought forth an iron mace as hard as a thunderbolt.
Then, out of fear, he who was called by that name ground [the child] and quickly cast him into the ocean;
the omniscient one, having learned the news, knew that the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis was at hand.
Having understood this, the enemy of Kaiṭabha set out for the sake of the pleasure of pilgrimage;
then followed the discus of the enemy of the gods, fierce as the orb of the sun.
The chariot and its golden banner suddenly vanished;
then, within the circle of the sky, which had become the color of a cat’s fur and was shrouded by headless torsos, [the sun appeared].
While the sun was scorching the entire expanse of the horizon and the wind was blowing,
Muṇḍa, with his face like a bird’s beak, appeared in every house of the Yādavas.
Having shown his face, he departed; though sought by voice, he was not seen.
The sound of the "cītkāra" man arose from the houses of the śārikā birds.
The royal highways were filled with the cries of vultures and jackals,
and at that time, the birth of animals became perverse.
Even when those terrible omens had arisen— such as jewels bursting spontaneously within their golden bindings in the treasuries— they remained free from apprehension.
The Vṛṣṇis shone; for indeed, their intellects did not fail them in times of destruction.
Then, when Kṛṣṇa had arrived at Prabhāsa, the Yādavas and Vṛṣṇis—
Having arrived at that very place, they held a grand festival;
they enjoyed themselves happily there in various gardens.
Addicted to the pleasures of song and dance, and seized by the eye of Time (Kāla),
they then became engrossed in the revelry of drinking within the Vṛṣṇi clan.
In a dispute concerning the battle, Sātyaki said to Kṛtavarman, the son of Śini: "O son of Hṛdika, you are a slayer of those who sleep; you are a nocturnal assassin."
He said to him: "By you was Bhūriśravas slain while he had undertaken a fast unto death.
Thus, from that dispute, there arose a most terrible battle among them.
Before those masses of creepers produced from that thunderbolt-club,
even a blade of grass there became as fierce as the staff of Brahmā due to its intoxication.
That woman, who was a festival for the eyes of their ladies, suddenly became a pestle for the destruction of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, serving as the site of their drinking bouts.
She herself became Death’s terrifying pavilion for the consumption of those who were being destroyed—
Sāmba, Gada, Cārudoṣṇa, Pradyumna, and Kṛtavarman.
When Aniruddha and Śaineya had been slain while Hari looked on, and the terrible destruction of the Vṛṣṇis had occurred, leaving only women remaining in the Yādava clan; (16.21)
Dvārakā wept aloud with streams of tears like severed necklaces;
then Śauri, overwhelmed by grief, went forth to see Haladhara.
Keśava sent Dāruka to inform Savyasācin,
taking Babhru with him for the protection of the women.
Having gone and taken leave of Janaka, the son of Rohiṇī approached [Rāma];
then Madhusūdana beheld [him] emerging from his mouth.
Then he [beheld] a thousand-headed white serpent, resembling a white mountain,
together with the nāgas led by Vāsuki who had come forward to meet him.
Having seen him enter the ocean and being honored once more by Varuṇa,
Janārdana, who knows the destiny of all beings, did not grieve.
For when non-existence exists within existence, how can there be stability for entities? When Balabhadra has merged into the infinite abode, even though the forest remains.
Having entered, the yogi slept with his vital breaths restrained;
a hunter, mistaking him for a deer, approached him as he was absorbed in his own inner light.
Thinking him to be a black antelope, the hunter struck him on the sole of his foot with a sharp-pointed arrow; thus Kṛṣṇa was killed by the hunter’s shaft.
He entered the supreme, eternal abode known as Nārāyaṇa,
while being honored by the gods, Siddhas, Ṛṣis, and Gandharvas, together with Śrī.
When Govinda had entered Viṣṇu, the world became agitated;
in the meantime, the destruction of the Yādavas was announced by Dāruka.
The Pāṇḍavas were overcome by supreme grief, terror, and dejection;
then, at the word of Yudhiṣṭhira, he whose horses are white [Aśvatthāman] departed for Dvārakā.
Accompanied by Dāruka alone, he set forth, fainting with grief;
he reached the city of the Yādavas, which was like a lotus pond filled with lotuses.
Beholding her with sorrow, like a Himalayan cave deserted by lions of the Vṛṣṇi clan and touched by a multitude of ominous portents.
To see Janaka, who was afflicted with grief for the enemy of Kaṃsa,
he entered the place where he was surrounded by the Vṛṣṇi women, who were making loud lamentations like the cries of cranes.
Seeing the sixteen thousand women who were the wives of the Lord of Kamalā, the father of Subhadrā’s son became overwhelmed with fear and lost his senses.
Seeing Vasudeva lying on the ground, lamenting, Pārtha too, overcome by grief, fell down as if struck by a thunderbolt.
"Where is Rāma? Where is Govinda? Where is Pradyumna? Where is Sātyaki?
Alas, the power of destiny is inexhaustible," Arjuna said.
There, the dense sound of dancing and singing, resonating with the jingling of jeweled bracelets,
arose incessantly like cascades that bring delight to the ears.
Right there, hearing the sound of the Vṛṣṇi women’s wailing,
Bībhatsu spent the night, which was devoid of any calamity, in prosperity.
Then at dawn, Vasudeva, whose son was dear to him, abandoned his beloved body, followed by Devakī and the foremost women of the household.
Then Pārtha, overwhelmed with grief, performed the cremation rites for the body of the foremost of the Sātvatas and offered the libations of water to all of them.
Then the son of Kuntī, taking Vajra— the descendant of Kṛṣṇa— and the wives of the Vṛṣṇis, set out, followed by Dāruka.
Then the ocean, hideous with the loud laughter of its conchs, swept away Dvāravatī with the circles of its arms of wide-spreading waves.
"Alas! Vṛṣṇipura has been swiftly swallowed by the ocean, as if out of greed for its jewels;
everything has followed after that man," so spoke the grieving people.
Taking the wife of the lions of the Vṛṣṇis, he who has white horses (Arjuna),
while proceeding toward Indraprastha, reached a formidable and treacherous forest.
There, the Dasyus were strong cowherds who lived by their cattle;
they had never before seen the beautiful women of the Sātvatas, who were like celestial nymphs.
Seeing the sky filled with masses of rays from jewels as flickering as lightning,
they fell under the power of greed and exerted themselves by force to seize them.
Seeing those cowherds rushing toward him with fierce clubs as their weapons,
the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow drew his Gāṇḍīva in fury.
Even though his enemies had been destroyed and he himself was struck down by the power of time,
he possessed no further strength to draw the bowstring once his arrows were exhausted.
His bow-staff became uncontrollable and led him into extreme suffering,
like a beautiful young wife to an old man who is poor.
As he was tormented by the fire of anger and pointlessly knitting his brows,
his arrows became as helpless as the servants of an undisciplined man.
Those multitudes of divine weapons departed somewhere in the battle, abandoning him,
disregarding their attachment to his qualities, just as rogues abandon a friend who is destitute.
Deprived of his vast resources, he sighed deeply;
like a generous man whose treasury is exhausted, his face was bowed down with embarrassment.
Then, when Pārtha had become speechless there due to the destruction of all his weapons, the women of the Vṛṣṇis and the city, devoid of discernment like forest-dwellers, carried him away.
But they showed no boldness toward the principal women; how could a base man, unworthy of such things, display vigor among those of great worth?
When their women were forcibly carried off by them, Dhanañjaya, his pride shattered,
set forth while casting envious glances at his own powerful arms.
Oh, how powerful is the goddess of impermanence in this saṃsāra!
Oh, how the sovereignty of all things culminates in essencelessness!
"Aha! Time is all-consuming; aha! The world has such diverse ripenings!
Victory over the conquered by cowherds! Thus did the people speak, as if struck by the sun of suffering.
Fie upon the Creator’s fondness for wondrous creation, which brings about the delusions and errors of this impermanent play! (Bhājana 16.60)
By him, Ākhaṇḍala and the other gods were defeated at Khāṇḍava;
by him, the enemy of Tripura was propitiated in battle at Kairāta.
Having defeated even that friend of Hari, those wretched cowherds carried off Viṣṇu’s wives; fie on the inexhaustible end of Time!
[He saw] Revatī, Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and likewise Jāmbavatī;
[he saw] Vajra, the grandson of the enemy of Kaṃsa, and other women of the Yadu clan.
Taking [the child], Phalguna entered Indraprastha in sorrow,
surrounded on all sides by the multitude of citizens who were weeping.
When Dhananjaya had departed for that very place after having installed Vajra in the kingdom, the queens,
followed by Satyabhāmā, entered the fire out of grief.
Traveling toward Hastināpura, Kirīṭin, afflicted by the separation from the Vṛṣṇis,
beheld Vyāsa in the forest, who knows the higher and lower nature of all things.
He reported to him the terrible destruction of the Vṛṣṇi clan, his own suffering,
and how he had been defeated on the road by cowherds after his bow was seized.
The sage, a treasury of knowledge, consoled him as he lay in a swoon and said:
"Son, all of this is but the manifestation of the play of Time."
Intellect, manifestations, enjoyments, powers, capacities, and virtues—in every way, by the movement of time, they are led to remain as nothing but memory. (Bhājana-vākya 16.69)
The sages would certainly not set their minds upon the renunciation of everything all at once,
were it not for the fact that the state of worldly existence is utterly devoid of any final satisfaction.
Thus addressed by the sage, Pārtha departed for Hastināpura,
deeply overwhelmed as he contemplated the power of that lion of the Vṛṣṇis.
Thus ends the Mausala Parva in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Śrī Kṣemendra.
